passages.t: ‘O God, You are my God’: thirst in a dry and weary land
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David, when he was in the Wilderness of Judah” (verse 1). The first words are personal. “O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water” (verse 1).

He remembers seeing God in worship. “So I have seen You in the sanctuary and beheld Your power and glory” (verse 2).

Then a line that sums up the whole psalm. “Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You” (verse 3). So he will praise God as long as he lives, lifting his hands (verse 4). And even in the desert he is full: “My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods; with joyful lips my mouth will praise You” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The Wilderness of Judah is the dry, rocky land between the hills of Judah and the Dead Sea. It gets very little rain. A person there without water is soon in danger. So when David speaks of thirst, he is not only using a picture. His body really was dry.

David was in that wilderness twice. As a young man he hid there from Saul (1 Samuel 23 and 24). Later, as king, he fled through it from his son Absalom, leaving the ark behind in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:25). Verse 11 calls him ‘the king’, so many readers favour the second time. The heading does not say which.

‘Loving devotion’ is hesed, God's love that keeps its promises (the book page explains the word). To call it ‘better than life’ is a huge claim. Life was the greatest good. David says God's love is greater still.

‘The richest of foods’ is, word for word, ‘fat and fatness’. In Israel the fat was the best part of a meal and of a sacrifice. In the desert, with nothing to eat, he feels as if he has been to a feast.

‘Earnestly I seek You’ is a verb that sounds like the Hebrew word for dawn. The old Greek translation took it as ‘I rise early to seek You’. In the early church Psalm 63 became the morning psalm. Christian church orders from the fourth century, such as the Apostolic Constitutions, name it for prayer at dawn.
passages.later:
Jesus also went into the wilderness, where “He was hungry” (Matthew 4:2).

He promised to meet the thirst of this psalm: “whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst” (John 4:14). And: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled” (Matthew 5:6).

Paul says something like ‘better than life’: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).
passages.hard: Is it right to say God's love is ‘better than life’? Does that mean life does not matter? No. The psalm loves life. David wants to praise God ‘as long as I live’. The point is about what is best of all. Life is a gift. The giver is better than the gift.
passages.asks:
Thirst is not a pleasant feeling, but it is a sign of life. If you feel dry toward God, that longing is itself a kind of prayer. This psalm puts words to it.

Notice the order. He is still in the desert when he says, ‘My soul is satisfied.’ The place has not changed. He has. Try praying verses 1 to 5 first thing in the morning, as Christians have done for many centuries.

passages.t: ‘Through the watches of the night’, and ‘My soul clings to You’
passages.happening:
Now it is night. “When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night. For You are my help; I will sing for joy in the shadow of Your wings” (verses 6 and 7).

Then one of the closest lines in the Psalms. “My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me” (verse 8).

There are still enemies. Those who want his life “will go into the depths of the earth” (verse 9). They will fall in battle and be left for wild animals (verse 10).

The psalm ends with the king. “But the king will rejoice in God; all who swear by Him will exult, for the mouths of liars will be shut” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The night was divided into ‘watches’, the times when guards took turns. To think of God ‘through the watches’ means lying awake all night. Many people know sleepless nights. David fills them with remembering God.

‘Clings’ is the same Hebrew word used when a man is ‘united to’ his wife (Genesis 2:24) and when Ruth ‘clung’ to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). It is the word for a bond that will not let go. And notice: he clings, and God's hand holds him up. Both are true at once.

Verse 10's ‘foxes’ are probably jackals, which ate the bodies left on a battlefield. To be left unburied was a disgrace. The prayer is for God's justice on those trying to kill him. The book page explains how such lines are read.

‘Swear by Him’ means taking oaths in God's name: people who are loyal to God. Their opposite is ‘liars’.
passages.later:
Jesus promised that no one can take his people from him: “No one can snatch them out of My hand” (John 10:28).

The wings picture appears in Ruth too, as Boaz blesses her: the God of Israel, “under whose wings you have taken refuge” (Ruth 2:12).
passages.asks:
If you lie awake at night, this psalm offers a way to use the hours. Not to force sleep, and not to worry, but to remember. What has God done? Where has his hand held you?

‘My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me.’ Your grip on God may feel weak. His grip on you is not. You can say verse 8 even on the night your strength is gone.
